To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) smoking is a normative behavior for adolescents; 2) adolescents who perceive that most other students smoke are most likely to smoke; 3) adolescents who perceive themselves as similar to the typical adolescent who smokes are most likely to start smoking; 4) the more adolescents believe that smoking is a norm for their age group, the more they smoke; 5) the greater the discrepancy between adolescents' beliefs about the typical adolescent who is their age and their own beliefs about themselves

the social context in which adolescents are exposed to smoking influences their adoption of smoking and that the more positive adolescents' beliefs are about the consequences of smoking the less likely they are to smoke.

(a) smoking adoption by adolescents is influenced by the social environment, and (b) smoking prevention programs that incorporate social influence principles and that are delivered by peers are more effective than other smoking prevention programs.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

social psychological theory and methods have provided a useful framework for understanding the processes of adolescent smoking acquisition, and that this understanding has been translated into effective prevention programs.

social psychological theory and methods have contributed to a better understanding of the social and psychological factors underlying adolescent smoking, to the development of more effective smoking intervention programs, and to the development of a more sophisticated conceptualization of the processes underlying smoking behavior.

social psychology has contributed to our understanding of how adolescents become smokers, why adolescents continue to smoke, and what can be done to prevent adolescents from starting to smoke or from continuing to smoke.
The main takeaway from our work is that

social psychological processes are central to understanding adolescent smoking adoption and cessation and that social psychological interventions are effective in preventing smoking among adolescents.
